## Psalm 78:1-24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Title: "A Maskil of Asaph"

**Traditional reading:** "Maskil" means an instructive or didactic poem (Hebrew *śākal*, "to be wise/prudent"), designed to impart wisdom. Asaph was the chief musician appointed by David (1 Chronicles 15:17–19), also called a prophet/seer (2 Chronicles 29:30). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/) ; StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note a).

**Reformed (Calvin):** The psalm was likely written long after David's death, since it celebrates the Davidic kingdom and brands Ephraim's kingdom as illegitimate. Nevertheless, Asaph or a later Asaphite poet is the inspired author speaking as a teacher, not God directly. — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**Anglican (Ellicott):** This is the first and longest "epi-didactic" psalm — combining narrative with instruction. It is a long confession of national failings, with special concern to establish why God rejected Ephraim in favour of Judah. The prominence given to the disruption of the kingdoms suggests a date around Hezekiah's time. — Ellicott, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/78.htm).

---

### v. 1 — "Give ear, O my people, to my instruction; listen to the words of my mouth."

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist opens with a call to careful attention. "My instruction" (Hebrew *torah*) here means teaching or doctrine broadly — not just the Mosaic Law. The address "my people" shows the love motivating the psalmist, not a claim to be God Himself. — Pulpit Commentary, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "When God gives his truth a tongue, and sends forth his messengers trained to declare his word with power, it is the least we can do to give them our ears and the earnest obedience of our hearts." Inclining the ears means earnest attention — "bow your stiff necks, lean forward to catch every syllable." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Reformed (Geneva Study Bible):** The prophet, under the name of a teacher, calls the people "his" and the doctrine "his," just as Paul calls the gospel "my gospel" (Romans 2:16; 16:25), though he was only its preacher. — Geneva Study Bible, StudyLight (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html).

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** "Psalm 78 begins with a principle sometimes neglected among those who would speak wisdom to others: you must first gain the attention of your listeners if you would teach them and reach them." He quotes Musculus (cited in Spurgeon): inclining the ears means hearing "with submission and reverence of mind, silent and earnest." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

---

### v. 2 — "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning."

**Traditional reading:** "Parable" (Hebrew *mashal*) means a comparison or proverb. "Dark sayings" or "things hidden" (Hebrew *chidoth*) refers to riddles — truths requiring reflection to discern. The facts of Israel's history contain an inner meaning, a "parable" for believers. — Ellicott, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/78.htm); Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Analogies are not only to be imagined, but are intended by God to be traced between the story of Israel and the lives of believers. Israel was ordained to be a type; the tribes and their marchings are living allegories traced by the hand of an all-wise providence." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Reformed (Calvin):** *Mashal* denotes "grave and striking sentences" — adages, proverbs, apophthegms; *chidoth* are "sayings which are pointed and worthy of special notice." The psalmist does not wrap his song in ambiguous language; he simply dignifies his subject to stimulate readers to weigh it more carefully. — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**All traditions note:** Matthew 13:35 quotes this verse as a prophecy fulfilled in Jesus' teaching in parables. All commentaries consulted affirm this connection.

---

### v. 3 — "that we have heard and known and our fathers have relayed to us."

**Traditional reading:** What the psalmist teaches is not novel; it is received tradition passed down through the covenant community. "Heard and known" confirms both oral transmission and personal verification. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/78.htm).

**Reformed (Calvin):** "Many things are rashly spread abroad which have no foundation in truth… It is, therefore, not without cause that the prophet, after having spoken of the things which he had heard, at the same time, refers in confirmation of their truth to undoubted testimony." The fathers referred to are not just any ancestors, but "those who were chosen to be God's peculiar people, and to whom the care of divine truth was intrusted." — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Tradition was of the utmost service to the people of God in the olden time, before the more sure word of prophecy had become complete and generally accessible." We now have the "less mutable testimony of written revelation," but this does not lessen our obligation to instruct children by word of mouth. — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### v. 4 — "We will not hide them from their children, but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might, and the wonders He has performed."

**Traditional reading:** This verse makes explicit the intergenerational obligation: what was received must be passed on. "Hide" implies a culpable silence. Three things must be transmitted: (1) the *praises* of the LORD (His worthiness of adoration), (2) His *might* (His power and greatness), and (3) His *wonderful works* (His power in active assistance to His people). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Our negligent silence shall not deprive our own and our father's offspring of the precious truth of God, it would be shameful indeed if we did so." He adds: "The more of parental teaching the better; ministers and Sabbath-school teachers were never meant to be substitutes for mother's tears and father's prayers." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Reformed (Calvin):** "By this means, all pretence of ignorance is removed; for it was the will of God that these things should be published from age to age without interruption; so that being transmitted from father to child in each family, they might reach even the last family of man." — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**Evangelical (Morgan, cited in Guzik):** "History should ever be the record of the works of God. That is to emphasize the important factor. History thus written, and thus taught, will so affect hope and memory in youth, as to constrain it to obedience to the God revealed; and this is the way of life for man and nation." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

---

### vv. 5–6 — "For He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which He commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the coming generation would know them — even children yet to be born — to arise and tell their own children."

**Traditional reading:** God's giving of His word (the "testimony" and "law") to Israel was one of His greatest "wonderful works." The command to teach children is rooted in Deuteronomy 6:6–9. Five generations appear in view: fathers → children → generation to come → their children → their children. — Adam Clarke, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Reformed (Calvin):** "He established a testimony in Jacob" refers to the written law: "God not only acquired a right to the Jews as his people by his mighty power, but… he also sealed up his grace, that the knowledge of it might never be obliterated." The law was given "not for one age only; but that the fathers should transmit it to their children, as if it were their rightful inheritance." This is why Paul calls the Church "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15). — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**Geneva Study Bible (Reformed):** "By the testimony and law, he means your law written, which they were commanded to teach their children, Deuteronomy 6:7." The children "would be like their father's: that is, in maintaining God's pure religion." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, notes d–e).

---

### v. 7 — "that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments."

**Traditional reading:** Faith (trust/confidence) comes first; then remembrance of God's works (which strengthens faith); then obedience (keeping commandments). This is the "sum of heavenly wisdom." — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**Geneva Study Bible (Reformed):** "He shows where the use of this doctrine exists: in faith, in the meditation of God's benefits, and in obedience." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note f).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Faith cometh by hearing. Those who know the name of the Lord will set their hope in him, and that they may be led to do so is the main end of all spiritual teaching." He adds: "Those who forget God's works are sure to fail in their own. He who does not keep God's love in memory is not likely to remember his law." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### v. 8 — "Then they will not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose heart was not loyal, whose spirit was not faithful to God."

**Traditional reading:** The purpose of intergenerational instruction is to break the cycle of rebellion. The fathers' sins are described as stubbornness, rebellion, an un-loyal (not "set aright") heart, and an unfaithful spirit — a focus on inner disposition, not merely outward actions. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Reformed (Calvin):** The fathers were "a rebellious [or apostatising] and a provoking generation." Calvin warns against the "perverse imitation of the fathers" — the natural human tendency to follow ancestral example. "It being a work of great difficulty to remove the disposition to this perverse imitation… the prophet employs a multiplicity of terms to set forth the aggravated wickedness of the fathers." — Calvin, BibleHub (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/78.htm).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Fathers stubborn in their own way, and rebellious against God's way, are sorry examples for their children… If our fathers were rebellious we must be better than they were, or else we shall perish as they did." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "Though these fathers were the seed of Abraham and the chosen people, yet he shows by their rebellion, provocation, falsehood, and hypocrisy, that the children should not follow their examples." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note g).

---

### v. 9 — "The archers of Ephraim turned back on the day of battle."

**Traditional reading — major interpretive crux:** No single historical battle is definitively identified. Several views exist:

**(a) Figurative/spiritual reading:** Many traditional commentators take this as a metaphor for spiritual failure, not literal cowardice. Ephraim, though well-armed ("equipped with bows"), turned back from loyalty to God's covenant. — Maclaren (cited in Enduring Word): "The reference to Ephraim in Psalm 78:9-11 is not to be taken as alluding to any cowardly retreat from actual battle. Psalm 78:9 seems to be a purely figurative way of expressing what is put without a metaphor in the two following verses. Ephraim's revolt from God's covenant was like the conduct of soldiers, well armed and refusing to charge the foe." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**(b) Ephraim as representative of all Israel:** "As the largest of the breakaway tribes, their subsequent history was to make them almost a symbol of backsliding and apostasy" (Kidner). The Geneva Study Bible agrees: "By Ephraim he means also the rest of the tribes, because they were most in number: whose punishment declares that they were unfaithful to God, and by their multitude and authority had corrupted all others." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note h).

**(c) Historical-critical:** Boice (Reformed) notes: "The incident referred to is not known. It was a time when 'Ephraim, though armed with bows, turned back on the day of battle.' Nothing exactly like this is found anywhere in the Old Testament." — cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**(d) Judges-era conflicts:** VanGemeren suggests the description "armed with bows" fits Ephraim's aggressiveness portrayed in Judges 8:1–3; 12:1–6. — cited in Enduring Word.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Applies the spiritual reading practically: "God makes spiritual resources available to His people for the spiritual conflicts they face (Ephesians 6:10-18). However, the effectiveness of those resources depends in some regard on their decision to actually make use of them." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "How often have we also, although supplied with every gracious weapon, failed to wage successful war against our sins, we have marched onward gallantly enough till the testing hour has come, and then 'in the day of battle' we have proved false to good resolutions and holy obligations." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### vv. 10–11 — "They failed to keep God's covenant and refused to live by His law. They forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them."

**Traditional reading:** These verses explain verse 9: the root of Ephraim's failure was covenant-breaking, law-refusing, and forgetting God's works. "Forgot" does not mean historically erased from memory, but practically — they did not so remember as to love, serve, and trust God. — Poole, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Had they remembered them they would have been filled with gratitude and inspired with holy awe: but the memory of God's mercies to them was as soon effaced as if written upon water." He adds: "Ere we condemn them, let us repent of our own wicked forgetfulness." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### v. 12 — "He worked wonders before their fathers in the land of Egypt, in the region of Zoan."

**Traditional reading:** "Zoan" (also known as Tanis) was a major city in the north-east Nile Delta, either identical with or near Rameses II's capital (Raamses), which the Israelites helped build (Exodus 1:11). The mention of Zoan underscores that God's wonders were performed publicly, in a prominent location. — Kidner, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "He proves that not only the posterity but also their forefathers were wicked and rebellious to God." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note i).

---

### v. 13 — "He split the sea and brought them through; He set the waters upright like a wall."

**Traditional reading:** Refers to the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14). The waters standing "like a wall" (literally "like a heap") recalls Exodus 15:8 and the Song of Moses. A "double wonder" (Spurgeon): the sea-bed, naturally impassable, was made a highway. — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "The nature of creatures is not their own intrinsically, but is retained or altered at the will of him who first created them. The Lord can cause those evils which threaten to overwhelm us to suspend their ordinary actions, and become innocuous to us." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### v. 14 — "He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night."

**Traditional reading:** The pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 40:36–38). The cloud was a "vast sun screen, rendering the fierce heat of the sun and the glare of the desert sand bearable" by day; by night it became a light. — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Older commentaries (Poole):** "A cloud; which was very comfortable, both for a shadow from the scorching heat of the climate and season, and for a companion and director in their journey." — cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "So constant was the care of the Great Shepherd that all night and every night the token of his presence was with his people. That cloud which was a shade by day was as a sun by night. Even thus the grace which cools and calms our joys, soothes and solaces our sorrows." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### vv. 15–16 — "He split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as abundant as the seas. He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers."

**Traditional reading:** Refers to at least two events: Rephidim (Exodus 17:6) and Kadesh (Numbers 20:1, 11) — hence the plural "rocks." The water was abundant — "as out of the great depths," gushing "from earth's innermost reservoirs." The supply was not a mere trickle but "torrents" and "streams" that followed the camp. — Poole, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/); Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "If we contemplate the abounding of divine grace we shall be lost in admiration. Mighty rivers of love have flowed for us in the wilderness." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### v. 17 — "But they continued to sin against Him, rebelling in the desert against the Most High."

**Traditional reading:** Despite all the miracles, Israel "sinned yet more" — outdoing former sins. The more God did, the more they complained. The word "rebelling" (or "provoking") uses the divine title "Most High" (*Elyon*), heightening the offence. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "It was bad enough to mistrust their God for necessaries, but to revolt against him in a greedy rage for superfluities was far worse. Ever is it the nature of the disease of sin to proceed from bad to worse; men never weary of sinning, but rather increase their speed in the race of iniquity." He adds: "Had not the Lord been so good they would not have been so bad. If he had wrought fewer miracles before, they would not have been so inexcusable in their unbelief." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "Their wicked malice could be overcome by no benefits, which were great and many." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note k).

---

### v. 18 — "They willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved."

**Traditional reading:** The testing consisted not merely in asking for food, but in demanding what their appetite craved (*food of their fancy* or *meat for their lust*). God had given manna; they wanted meat (Numbers 11:4–10, 18–23, 31–34). They were dissatisfied with what God provided and implied He was unable to do more. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "Then to require more than is necessary, and to separate God's power from his will, is to tempt God." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note l).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "The sin began in their hearts, but it soon reached their tongues. What they at first silently wished for, they soon loudly demanded with menaces, insinuations, and upbraidings." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

---

### vv. 19–20 — "They spoke against God, saying, 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness? When He struck the rock, water gushed out and torrents raged. But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?'"

**Traditional reading:** This is the climax of their unbelief. They admitted God had split the rock (vv. 15–16) — they conceded the past miracle — yet questioned whether He could give bread and meat. The phrase "prepare a table" echoes Psalm 23:5 ("You prepare a table before me"), forming a "shining contrast" between David's trust and Israel's unbelief. — Kidner, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "From this verse we learn that unbelief of God is a slander against him." He calls their argument "superabundant folly and insolence" — "If they had argued, 'can he not give flesh?' the argument would have been reasonable, but they ran into insanity; when, having seen many marvels of omnipotence, they dared to insinuate that other things were beyond the divine power." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Guzik recounts the story of J. Edwin Orr, who in 1933 left a good job with only 2 shillings and 8 pence, trusting God to provide as he travelled Britain calling for revival. His first book, titled *Can God—?*, was based on Psalm 78:19 and sold hundreds of thousands of copies. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "Thus when we give place to sin, we are moved to doubt God's power, unless he is always ready to serve our lust." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note m).

---

### vv. 21–22 — "Therefore the LORD heard and was filled with wrath; so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel, because they did not believe God or rely on His salvation."

**Traditional reading:** God heard directly — He "dwelt among them in the holy place, and, therefore, they insulted him to his face" (Spurgeon). The "fire" likely alludes to the literal fire at Taberah (Numbers 11:1–3), but also represents divine wrath generally. The root sin is identified: unbelief and failure to trust His salvation. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "This is the master sin, the crying sin. Like Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, it sins and makes Israel to sin; it is in itself evil and the parent of evils. It was this sin which shut Israel out of Canaan, and it shuts myriads out of heaven." He adds a striking pastoral warning: "In the text it appears as if all Israel's other sins were as nothing compared with this; this is the peculiar spot which the Lord points at, the special provocation which angered him. From this let every unbeliever learn to tremble more at his unbelief than at anything else. If he be no fornicator, or thief, or liar, let him reflect that it is quite enough to condemn him that he trusts not in God's salvation." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "That is, in his fatherly providence, by which he cares for his, and provides sufficiently." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note n).

---

### vv. 23–24 — "Yet He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of the heavens. He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven."

**Traditional reading:** Despite their unbelief (v. 22), God responded with grace and provision — the "Yet" is pivotal. "Opened the doors of heaven" is a dramatic image of divine abundance. The manna is called "grain from heaven" (literally "corn of heaven"), described as "angels' food" in verse 25 (BSB: "grain from heaven"). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Such a marvel ought to have rendered unbelief impossible: when clouds become granaries, seeing should be believing, and doubts should dissolve." He adds that manna was "round, like coriander seed, and hence was rightly called corn; it did not rise from the earth, but descended from the clouds, and hence the words of the verse are literally accurate." — Spurgeon, Treasury of David (http://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps078.php).

**Geneva Study Bible:** "So that they had that which was necessary and sufficient: but their lust made them cover that which they knew God had denied them." — Geneva Study Bible (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/psalms-78.html, note o).

**New Testament connection:** In John 6:31, the crowd quotes Psalm 78:24 to Jesus ("He gave them bread from heaven to eat"), hoping He would keep providing miraculous bread. They thus "fulfilled it in a negative way, showing the same ingratitude and willingness to test God that Israel showed in the wilderness." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/).

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Distinctives

| Tradition | Source | Distinctive Emphasis |
|-----------|--------|---------------------|
| **Reformed (Calvin)** | Calvin, BibleHub | God's sovereignty in establishing the testimony; the law as "rightful inheritance"; the Church as "pillar and ground of truth"; emphasis on God's secret work in turning hearts |
| **Reformed (Geneva)** | Geneva Study Bible | Compact doctrinal notes stressing covenant, written law transmitted through generations, and the distinction between God's provision and human lust |
| **Baptist (Spurgeon)** | Treasury of David | Vivid, devotional, Christ-centred application; unbelief as "the master sin"; pastoral urgency for parental instruction; personal application of Israel's failures to the believer's heart |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik)** | Enduring Word | Practical application to spiritual warfare (Eph. 6); emphasis on using available spiritual resources; edifying illustrations (J. Edwin Orr); accessible modern exposition |
| **Anglican (Ellicott)** | Ellicott, BibleHub | Focus on historical-critical questions: date, authorship, the disruption of the kingdoms, Ephraim vs. Judah; the "epi-didactic" genre of psalm |
